catalog_quote: There are three main level tones—High, Mid, and Low, though Mid tone may often be regarded as lowered High; there is also a Falling tone which seems to constitute a separate toneme. In PAKOT there is also a Rising tone. Tone is both lexical and grammatical, and in all languages there are Tone Classes ... It has not been possible to tone-mark all examples, especially in BARI. 2b. Stress Stress falls normally on the Stem syllable of words. In BARI there is significant shifting of stress in certain circumstances: Tone Class 1 Tone Class 2 nan Io 't6togu I am cutting nan Io 'yiymnga I am listening nan 19 t6't6gu (emphatic) nan Id y1'yinga (emphatic) ... On other occasions it is hard to determine whether tone or stress is the dominant factor: d5 nyanyar nan, lit. you like which? tipo he is not coming

new_statements.rule_in_words: Group-level statement for the Paranilotic (Eastern Nilotic) languages treated together, Bari-based: the languages have three level tones (High, Mid, Low) plus a Falling toneme, tone being lexical and grammatical; word stress normally falls on the stem syllable (i.e. a morphologically determined placement), and in Bari stress shifts off the stem-initial syllable under emphasis (tɔ'tɔgu, yi'yiŋŋa vs. 'tɔtɔgu, 'yiŋŋa); elsewhere it is 'hard to determine whether tone or stress is the dominant factor'. Nothing Kakwa-specific: the only Kakwa remarks recovered concern consonants (z in Congo Kakwa = j elsewhere), verb-form variants and gender of personal names marked by tone.
new_statements.exceptions: In Bari 'significant shifting of stress in certain circumstances' (emphatic forms move stress from the first stem syllable to the second); footnote contrasts Pakot (Kalenjin) 'kara ku:kat, with no slurring'; p. 450: cases where tone and stress cannot be separated (dɔ nyanyar nan 'you like which?' vs 'you like me?'; tipo vs ti pɔ). An 'Observation' adds that tone and stress patterns 'may vary widely even between dialects' (Nandi vs Kipsigis).
new_statements.identity_note: Tucker & Bryan 1966 treat Kakwa only as an appendage of Bari ('BARI (with some notes on KAKWA)') inside a comparative Paranilotic chapter; the stress and tone statements are for the group with Bari examples, and the Kakwa notes recovered (Congo Kakwa z = j elsewhere; verb-form variants rem/rem-o/rem-bu; personal-name gender marked by tone) say nothing about stress. Spagnolo 1933 is a grammar of Bari (bari1284), and its open copy is a two-page vernacular text sample.

Section III 'Tone' (journal pp. 11-13, pp. 16-18) describes Kakuwâ as a tone language with two level tones (High, Low) plus a Falling tone, lexical and grammatical tone, and downstep; Section IV notes first syllables generally carry a single level tone while final syllables may carry complex tones.
No phonology content; cites Onziga & Gilley 2012 only.
